summary: Asks the IEEE 802.15 Assigned Numbers Authority to allocate an Information Element number to the IETF in the IEEE 802.15.4 registry. It also describes how that element is formatted so that subtypes can be defined under it.

eli5.summary: A big club keeps a list of numbered badges. The IETF asks for one badge of its own and explains how it will use it.

questions: how to get an ieee 802.15.4 ie number
how to allocate ietf ie subtypes
subtitle: A reserved slot in 802.15.4 for IETF-defined protocols.

tldr.problem: IETF protocols running on low-power wireless networks need a standard way to add their own metadata to IEEE 802.15.4 frames. The IEEE 802.15.4 standard defines Information Elements for this, but the IETF had to request a dedicated element number.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC asks the IEEE 802.15 Assigned Numbers Authority to allocate one Information Element (ID 5) for the IETF and specifies how subtypes within that element can be defined. Working groups like 6TiSCH can then request subtype IDs from an IANA registry.
tldr.outcome: The IEEE granted IE 5 to the IETF. The RFC created an IANA registry for subtype IDs (0 reserved, 1–200 unassigned, 201–255 experimental), enabling future IETF protocols to coexist within the same IE.

today: RFC 8137 is an Internet Standard and has not been obsoleted. The IEEE 802.15 Assigned Numbers Authority allocated IE number 5 to the IETF as requested. The IANA registry for IETF IE subtype IDs is active and ready for allocation.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
IEEE Std 802.15.4 defines Information Elements (IEs), which are optional fields in 802.15.4 frames that extend the standard in an interoperable way. Each IE has an ID, a length field, and content. Two types exist: Header IEs (never encrypted, processed by the MAC) and Payload IEs (may be encrypted and authenticated).

IETF protocols that run on 802.15.4 networks—like those designed by the 6TiSCH and 6lo working groups for IPv6 over low-power wireless—need a place to insert their own metadata into frames. The RFC requests that the IEEE 802.15 Assigned Numbers Authority (ANA) allocate one Payload IE exclusively for IETF use.
sections.eli5: Ethernet frames have slots for extra info. Low-power wireless uses the same idea. IETF needed one of those slots, so they asked the IEEE for it.

sections.title: Subtype Format
sections.content:
The IETF IE content begins with a 1-byte Subtype ID field, followed by the actual subtype content. Subtype ID 0 is reserved for future extensibility (in case longer IDs are needed). The maximum Payload IE content is 2047 octets. Frames can contain multiple IETF IEs with the same or different subtypes.

This format avoids the need to define the internal nesting structure of the IETF IE itself. The 802.15.4 standard's Length field already indicates how much space is available, so subtype content length is simply calculated from that.
sections.eli5: The IETF badge has a small field at the front that says which type of information comes next, then the information itself. Different groups put different information in their part of the badge.

sections.title: IANA Registry for Subtypes
sections.content:
The RFC creates the "IEEE Std 802.15.4 IETF IE Subtype IDs" registry. Allocations follow Expert Review (RFC 5226). The initial allocation is: 0 (Reserved), 1–200 (Unassigned), 201–255 (Experimental Use).

This structure ensures that any IETF working group needing a subtype ID can request one through IANA, and implementations can skip unknown IETF IEs because the length field is always known. The separate Vendor Specific IEs already defined in 802.15.4 eliminate the need to reserve any subtype IDs for vendor-specific uses.
sections.eli5: IANA keeps a list of which groups have claimed which sub-badges. New groups can ask IANA for one, and there's even a section for experiments.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
The security of protocols using the IETF IE must be described in the documents requesting subtype allocations. 802.15.4 enforces security per IE type, so all IETF IEs have the same security-level requirements regardless of subtype. If different subtypes need different security, higher-layer processing SHOULD perform separate security policy checking based on the subtype ID in addition to MAC-layer checks.

Since IETF protocols operate above the MAC level, this separation of concerns is manageable.
sections.eli5: The wireless standard handles basic security for the whole badge, but each sub-badge might need its own rules, so the software using them has to check those too.
